title: Core Java
description: Language, collections, concurrency and the JVM: the questions that start almost every Java interview. Write your answer first, then compare it with the model answer.

questions.title: The equals and hashCode contract
questions.prompt: Why must you override `hashCode` whenever you override `equals`? What breaks if you do not?
questions.answer:
The contract says: equal objects must have equal hash codes. `HashMap` and `HashSet` first use `hashCode` to pick a bucket and only then call `equals` inside the bucket. If two equal objects have different hash codes they land in different buckets, so `set.contains(copy)` returns false, duplicates appear in a `HashSet`, and `map.get(equalKey)` misses.

The reverse is allowed: unequal objects may share a hash code (a collision), which only costs speed. Use the same fields in both methods, prefer immutable keys (changing a field after insertion loses the entry), and let a `record` or `Objects.hash(...)` generate them.
questions.hint: Think about how a HashMap finds a key: which method runs first?

questions.title: How does HashMap work?
questions.prompt: Describe how a `HashMap` stores and finds an entry, what happens on a collision, and what changed in Java 8.
questions.answer:
A `HashMap` is an array of buckets. `put(key, value)` computes `hashCode`, spreads its bits, and takes `hash & (n - 1)` as the bucket index. If the bucket is empty the entry is stored there; otherwise the entries in the bucket are compared with `equals` and either one is replaced or the new one is appended (a collision, handled by chaining).

When the number of entries exceeds `capacity * loadFactor` (default 0.75) the table doubles and entries are redistributed. Since **Java 8**, a bucket with 8 or more entries (and a table of at least 64 slots) is converted into a balanced tree, so the worst case lookup is O(log n) instead of O(n). Average `get` and `put` are O(1). It allows one `null` key, is not thread-safe, and iteration order is not guaranteed.

questions.title: String immutability and the pool
questions.prompt: Why are Java strings immutable? What does `new String("a") == "a"` return, and why?
questions.answer:
A `String` is immutable so that it can be shared safely between threads, cached (its hash code is computed once, which makes it a good `HashMap` key), kept in the **string pool**, and used for security-sensitive values such as class names and file paths without anyone changing them after validation.

Literals are interned in the pool, so `"a" == "a"` is true. `new String("a")` always creates a new object on the heap, so `new String("a") == "a"` is **false**, while `.equals` is true. Always compare strings with `equals`. Use `StringBuilder` for building strings in a loop, because `+=` creates a new string each time.

questions.title: Checked versus unchecked exceptions
questions.prompt: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions, and which should you use in your own code?
questions.answer:
**Checked** exceptions (subclasses of `Exception` that are not `RuntimeException`, such as `IOException`) must be caught or declared with `throws`; the compiler forces the caller to think about them. **Unchecked** exceptions (`RuntimeException` and `Error`, such as `NullPointerException` or `IllegalArgumentException`) need no declaration.

Guideline: use unchecked exceptions for programming errors and for failures the caller cannot reasonably recover from; use checked ones only when the caller can and should react. Modern frameworks, Spring included, mostly use unchecked exceptions, because checked ones clutter signatures and break lambdas. Never swallow an exception silently, and keep the cause when you wrap one.

questions.title: Interface or abstract class?
questions.prompt: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface now that interfaces can have default methods?
questions.answer:
An **interface** defines a capability or contract; a class can implement many. Since Java 8 it can have `default` and `static` methods, and since 9 `private` methods, but no instance state.

An **abstract class** can hold state (fields), constructors, and non-public members, and provides a partial implementation for a family of related classes, but a class can extend only one. Choose an abstract class when subclasses share state or a template-method skeleton, and an interface when you are defining a role that unrelated classes can play. Prefer interfaces for public APIs, since they leave the single inheritance slot free; use `sealed` interfaces to restrict who may implement them.

questions.title: What does volatile guarantee?
questions.prompt: What does `volatile` do, and what does it not do? Give an example where it is not enough.
questions.answer:
`volatile` guarantees **visibility** and **ordering**: a write to a volatile variable is visible to every thread that later reads it, and the write happens-before that read, so the JVM and CPU may not cache or reorder it away. It does **not** make compound actions atomic.

`volatile int count; count++;` is still a race: it reads, adds and writes in three steps, so two threads can lose an update. Use `AtomicInteger`, `synchronized` or a lock for that. Good uses of `volatile`: a stop flag, or safely publishing an immutable object reference (the double-checked locking singleton needs it).

questions.title: synchronized or ReentrantLock?
questions.prompt: Compare `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock`. When is the lock class worth it?
questions.answer:
`synchronized` is simple, built into the language, releases the monitor automatically (even on an exception), and is heavily optimised by the JVM. `ReentrantLock` offers more: `tryLock()` (with a timeout), interruptible acquisition, optional fairness, multiple `Condition` queues, and a `ReadWriteLock` or `StampedLock` for read-heavy data.

You must unlock in a `finally` block. Default to `synchronized` or higher level tools (`ConcurrentHashMap`, atomics, executors); reach for `ReentrantLock` when you need a try-lock, a timeout, or separate wait conditions. With virtual threads, prefer `ReentrantLock` over long `synchronized` blocks around blocking calls on older JDKs, because pinning could hold a carrier thread.

questions.title: ConcurrentHashMap
questions.prompt: How is `ConcurrentHashMap` different from `Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>())` and from `Hashtable`?
questions.answer:
`Hashtable` and `synchronizedMap` lock the **entire map** for every operation, so threads queue up, and iterating still needs external synchronisation. `ConcurrentHashMap` allows concurrent reads without locking and locks only a bin (or uses CAS) for writes, so many threads can work at once. Its iterators are weakly consistent and never throw `ConcurrentModificationException`.

It offers atomic compound operations: `putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent`, `merge`, `compute`. A sequence like `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)` is still a race even on a `ConcurrentHashMap`; use `putIfAbsent`. It does not allow `null` keys or values.

questions.title: How does garbage collection work?
questions.prompt: Explain how the JVM decides an object can be collected and why most collectors are generational.
questions.answer:
An object is garbage when it is **unreachable** from the GC roots (thread stacks, static fields, JNI references). The collector traces from the roots, marks reachable objects, and reclaims the rest; having no references is enough, even if a cycle of dead objects point to each other.

**Generational** collectors rely on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. New objects go in a small *young generation* that is collected often and cheaply by copying survivors; objects that survive several collections are promoted to the *old generation*, collected less often. Modern collectors: **G1** (default; region based, pause-time goals), **ZGC** and **Shenandoah** (very short pauses with concurrent compaction). A memory leak in Java means objects that are still reachable but no longer needed, such as entries in a static map.

questions.title: Generics and type erasure
questions.prompt: What is type erasure, and what limits does it impose? What does PECS mean?
questions.answer:
Generics are checked by the compiler, then the type arguments are **erased**: `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both plain `List` at runtime, with casts inserted by the compiler. Consequences: you cannot write `new T()`, `new T[10]`, `instanceof List<String>`, or overload methods that differ only in type arguments, and generic type information is not available by reflection (except in some signatures).

**PECS** (producer extends, consumer super) guides wildcards. If a collection *produces* values you read, use `? extends T` (read only). If it *consumes* values you write into, use `? super T`. For example `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)`.

questions.title: Streams: laziness and pitfalls
questions.prompt: What does it mean that streams are lazy? Name two pitfalls of using them.
questions.answer:
Intermediate operations (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`) only describe a pipeline; nothing runs until a **terminal** operation (`collect`, `forEach`, `count`, `findFirst`). Elements flow through the pipeline one at a time, and short-circuiting operations such as `findFirst` or `limit` stop early. A stream can be consumed only once.

Pitfalls: (1) **side effects** in `map` or `filter` (modifying outside state) make behaviour unpredictable, especially with `parallel()`; (2) **`parallelStream()`** uses the shared common pool and only helps for large, CPU-bound, independent work: for small or blocking tasks it is slower. Also: avoid streams where a simple loop is clearer, and do not rely on `peek` for logic.

questions.title: Using Optional well
questions.prompt: How should `Optional` be used, and where should it not be used?
questions.answer:
`Optional<T>` models a return value that may be absent, so callers are forced to handle the empty case. Use `map`, `flatMap`, `orElse`, `orElseGet`, `orElseThrow` instead of `isPresent()` plus `get()`.

Do not use it for fields, method parameters, or collection elements (return an empty collection instead of an `Optional<List<T>>`), do not call `get()` without checking, and never return `null` from a method whose type is `Optional`. `orElse(expensive())` always evaluates its argument; use `orElseGet(() -> expensive())` to compute lazily.

questions.title: Virtual threads
questions.prompt: What are virtual threads (Java 21), when do they help, and when do they not?
questions.answer:
A virtual thread is a lightweight thread scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier (platform) threads. When it blocks on I/O or a `Lock`, it is unmounted and the carrier runs another virtual thread, so you can have millions of them and write simple blocking code instead of reactive callbacks.

They help with **I/O-bound, high concurrency** workloads: web servers handling many slow requests, calls to databases and remote services. They do not speed up **CPU-bound** work (you still have a fixed number of cores), they should not be pooled (create one per task, e.g. `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`), and shared resources still need limits (a semaphore or connection pool) so you do not overload a database. Avoid holding `synchronized` around blocking calls on older JDKs, where it pins the carrier thread.

questions.title: Records, sealed types and pattern matching
questions.prompt: What is a `record`, and how do sealed interfaces and pattern matching in `switch` work together?
questions.answer:
A `record` is a transparent, immutable data carrier: `record Point(int x, int y) {}` generates the constructor, accessors, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. It cannot extend a class, but can implement interfaces and add methods and validation in a compact constructor.

A **sealed** interface lists the permitted implementations: `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}`. A `switch` over a sealed type with record patterns, `case Circle(double r) -> ...`, is checked for **exhaustiveness** by the compiler, so adding a new implementation causes a compile error wherever it is not handled. Together they model algebraic data types without the visitor pattern.

questions.title: The Java Memory Model and happens-before
questions.prompt: What is the happens-before relation, and name three ways to establish it.
questions.answer:
Without synchronisation, one thread's writes may not be visible to another, or may appear reordered, because of CPU caches and compiler optimisations. The **Java Memory Model** defines *happens-before*: if action A happens-before action B, then A's effects are visible to B.

Ways to establish it: (1) **unlocking a monitor** happens-before every later locking of the same monitor (`synchronized`, `Lock`); (2) a **write to a volatile** variable happens-before every later read of it; (3) `Thread.start()` happens-before everything in the started thread, and everything in a thread happens-before another thread's successful `join()` on it. Executors, `ConcurrentHashMap` and `CountDownLatch` also provide guarantees. A data race (two threads touching the same variable, one writing, with no happens-before) has undefined visibility.
